meta.title: PagedAttention: KV-cache block tables, fragmentation, copy-on-write, preemption
meta.subject: Computer science

story.title: How a 1962 operating-system trick fit 2–4× more conversations on a GPU

tldr: An LLM's KV cache grows one row per token and nobody knows the final length. Old servers reserved a max-length slab per request and used only 20–38% of it. PagedAttention cuts the cache into fixed 16-token blocks placed anywhere in GPU memory, tracked by a per-request block table, allocated on demand and shared copy-on-write.
why: Why it matters: decode is memory-bound, so throughput scales with how many sequences fit. Packing KV well gave vLLM 2–4× throughput, and every major open serving engine now pages its KV cache.

cards.title: Restaurant tables, not one long bench
cards.brief:
A cautious host reserves 20 bench seats for a party of 3, and the room fills with empty seats. PagedAttention gives each party small 4-seat tables, handed out as needed, anywhere in the room. A card records which tables are theirs.

Nearly every seat gets used, so one GPU serves 2–4× more conversations.

cards.title: Six things to know first
cards.brief:
• KV cache: past tokens' keys/values, one row per token per layer.
  • Decode is memory-bound: throughput comes from big batches.
  • OS paging: page tables, copy-on-write, swap. The whole idea is borrowed from here.

cards.title: Where it runs and what you actually touch
cards.brief: Default in vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, TGI, SGLang. You never touch the block table; you set --gpu-memory-utilization, --max-model-len, --block-size and prefix caching. Watch the startup log line # GPU blocks.

cards.title: "Virtual memory for the KV cache" hides five things
cards.brief: The attention kernel itself changes. Fragmentation drops but doesn't vanish. On-demand allocation can run out mid-answer. Sharing is a second win and a security hole. And no hardware MMU is involved.

cards.title: Contiguous reservation wastes 60–80% of KV memory
cards.brief:
Output length is unknown, so old servers reserved max_len per request. Three kinds of waste: reservation, internal and external fragmentation. Even an oracle that knows every length loses to paging by 1.7–2.7×.

Includes an interactive pool visualizer.

cards.title: OS paging, and where the analogy breaks
cards.brief: Request = process, block = page, block table = page table, parallel samples = fork(). But there's no MMU or TLB, every step reads every block, and KV can be recomputed instead of swapped.

cards.title: One prompt, block by block
cards.brief:
7-token prompt, B = 4 → blocks [7, 1]. Token 9 fills #1, so allocate #3 → table [7, 1, 3]. A second request shares #7 and #1 (refcount 2); the first write copies only the tail block.

7-step interactive walkthrough inside.

cards.title: Waste is bounded by one block, and softmax merges exactly
cards.brief:
Expected tail waste is (B−1)/2 slots per sequence: about 1.25% at B = 16. Per-block softmax partials (max, sum, weighted value) merge with rescaling, so paged attention is bit-for-bit the same math as contiguous.

Block-size explorer inside.

cards.title: Append-only + read-in-order = no contiguity needed
cards.brief: Remove any piece and something breaks: no block table → back to 20–38%; no refcounts → no sharing; no CoW → siblings corrupt each other; no preemption → OOM. Fixed-size blocks make external fragmentation impossible.

cards.title: Block size, memory fraction, preemption mode
cards.brief: Small blocks mean less waste but more indirection; vLLM picks 16, TRT-LLM 128. Alternatives: vAttention (hardware virtual memory, unmodified kernels), SGLang radix trees, and lossy KV compression.

cards.title: Preemption thrash and timing side channels
cards.brief: Many sequences need a block at once → the newest is evicted, recomputed, evicted again. Shared prefix caches leak other users' prompts through time-to-first-token; 7 API providers shared caches globally (ICML'25).

cards.title: How real engines deviate from the paper
cards.brief: vLLM V1: recompute (not swap), prefix caching on by default, chunked prefill. TRT-LLM: 128-token blocks, reuse only after the producer finishes. Mooncake / LMCache move blocks across GPU, DRAM and SSD.

cards.title: From packing KV to placing, pruning and protecting it
cards.brief: vAttention (ASPLOS'25), DistServe (OSDI'24), Mooncake, KIVI 2-bit KV, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, LMCache, PagedEviction. Packing is solved; the fight moved to where KV lives and who may share it.

cards.title: What nobody has solved yet
cards.brief: Admission without thrash under unknown lengths. Prefix sharing that's provably private. Whether hardware VM retires software block tables. No head-to-head measurement on real public traces.

cards.title: Atlas paging (1962) → vLLM (2023) → today
cards.brief: Virtual memory → Orca's iteration batching → PagedAttention → radix-tree reuse, prefix caching, vAttention, disaggregation, lossy KV.

cards.title: Simulate a KV pool in 30 seconds
cards.brief: python3 kv_alloc_sim.py: contiguous/max hits 32% utilization, paged/16 hits 96.9%, matching the paper's 96.3%. Then try a watermark and watch preemptions drop.

cards.title: Test yourself
cards.brief: 22 questions from mechanism to open research. Reveal, then mark ✓ or ✗; marks feed your progress ring.

cards.title: Three dives that build on this
cards.brief: Chunked prefill (Sarathi-Serve) · prefill/decode disaggregation · KV-cache timing side channels.

cards.title: Papers, code and docs
cards.brief: 19 papers, 8 code/doc references, plus the list of claims I couldn't verify.

cold.q: Before 2023, what share of that KV memory held actual tokens?
cold.reveal: In pre-2023 serving systems, only 20–38%. The rest was reserved for words that were never written, or stranded in gaps between requests. A 2023 paper got it to 96.3%, and every major open serving engine now works the same way.

oracle.q: Suppose the old server knew every answer's exact length in advance and reserved exactly that. How does paging compare?
oracle.reveal: Even the oracle version of Orca loses by 1.7–2.7× on ShareGPT. Exact reservations still leave gaps between requests (external fragmentation), and nothing can be shared.

cow.q: 4 samples share a 30-token prompt, block size 16. On the first decode step, how many blocks get copied?
cow.reveal: 3. Block 0 is full and stays shared. Block 1 holds 14 tokens with refcount 4: the first three writers each copy it, and the last one writes in place.

tail.q: Block size 16, sequences average 600 tokens. What share of KV memory is wasted in the half-empty last blocks?
tail.reveal: About 1.25%. Each sequence wastes (B−1)/2 = 7.5 slots on average, out of 600. With B = 512 it would be about 42%.

leak.q: A 2025 audit timed LLM APIs to detect one user's prompt cache speeding up another user's request. How many providers shared a cache across all users?
leak.reveal: 7, including OpenAI (Gu et al., ICML'25). A cache hit returns faster, so an attacker can test whether someone else recently sent a given prompt.

questions.q: What does the kernel load, in order, for token 9 in the trace?
questions.a: It reads the table [7, 1, 3] and seq_len 9: physical #7 (4 tokens), #1 (4 tokens), then #3 with 1 valid token. It computes block-local max and sum and merges them with online-softmax rescaling. Loads are coalesced within a block; only the jumps between blocks are indirect.

questions.q: When does vLLM allocate a new physical block?
questions.a: At prefill, ⌈prompt/B⌉ blocks. During decode, only when the last block is full and a token must be written. It pops any free block id and appends it to the table. If none is free, the scheduler preempts first.

questions.q: n=4 samples, prompt 30, B=16: blocks copied on the first decode?
questions.a: Block 0 is full and block 1 is partial (14 tokens), both refcount 4. The first three writers to block 1 see refcount > 1 and copy; the fourth writes in place. 3 copies, and block 0 is never copied.

questions.q: Finished blocks with prefix caching on vs off?
questions.a: Off: refcount 0, blocks go to the free pool with meaningless contents. On: full blocks keep their hash in an LRU free queue, reusable by a matching hash chain or evicted under pressure. Tail blocks evict first.

questions.q: Why do fixed-size blocks eliminate external fragmentation?
questions.a: Every allocation asks for exactly one block, so any free block satisfies it. "Enough free memory, but no hole big enough" can't happen.

questions.q: Why does an oracle contiguous allocator still lose?
questions.a: External fragmentation (79% of free memory outside the largest hole in the simulation), head-of-line blocking, and no sharing of prompt blocks.

questions.q: Why B = 16?
questions.a: Tail waste of about (B−1)/2 favors small B; coalescing, fewer lookups and fewer tiny swaps favor large B. The paper's sweep found 16–128 best on ShareGPT and 16–32 on Alpaca. TRT-LLM picks 128 for its kernels.

questions.q: Why is preemption all-or-nothing per group?
questions.a: Every step reads every block, so there's no cold subset, and a sequence missing any block can't run. Group members share blocks, so they're gang-scheduled and preempted together.

questions.q: Why hash only full blocks, and why chain the parent?
questions.a: A partial block's contents still change. KV at position t depends on every earlier token, so identical 16 tokens after a different prefix have different K,V. The parent hash encodes the whole prefix.

questions.q: Remove refcounts but keep block tables?
questions.a: The packing benefit stays, but sharing is unsafe because you can't know when to free or copy. You lose parallel-sampling and beam savings (37.6–66.3% for beams) and prefix caching.

questions.q: If output lengths were known exactly, is paging still worth it?
questions.a: Yes, though less so. External fragmentation (unless you compact by copying) and lack of sharing remain. vLLM's gain shrinks from 2.7–8× (vs Orca-Max) to 1.7–2.7× (vs Orca-Oracle).

questions.q: With a cheap hardware MMU for GPU memory?
questions.a: Software tables and kernel indirection disappear (vAttention-like). On-demand mapping, refcounts or CoW, preemption policy and prefix hashing remain.

questions.q: How do you extract another tenant's prompt from a shared prefix cache?
questions.a: Probe guessed prefixes and measure TTFT; a fast response means a hit. Extend block by block or token by token (Early Bird). Larger B means more candidates per step. Defenses: salts, isolation, noise.

questions.q: Design a workload that maximizes thrash.
questions.a: Bursts of short prompts with long outputs, high max_num_seqs, no watermark. Sequences cross block boundaries together, the pool empties, the newest are recomputed and evicted again. Each cycle costs a full prefill.

questions.q: How can a prefix-hash collision fail?
questions.a: Request B reuses A's KV: wrong outputs conditioned on A's text, and possible leakage of A's content. That's why the default is SHA-256 with a warning about xxhash.

questions.q: Relation to fork() and where it fails?
questions.a: Samples are forked processes sharing refcounted pages copied on write. There are no MMU faults (the scheduler checks refcounts), no locality-driven paging, and contents can be recomputed.

questions.q: How does disaggregation depend on blocks?
questions.a: KV moves between prefill and decode nodes and tiers (RDMA, DRAM, SSD) as fixed-size blocks, mapped into the decoder's table without contiguity.

questions.q: How does KIVI compose with paging?
questions.a: They're orthogonal: fewer bytes per token, so more tokens per pool. Key quantization works on token groups, which interacts with block boundaries and the full-precision residual tail.

questions.q: Online softmax and FlashAttention?
questions.a: Same running max and sum merge. FlashAttention tiles for SRAM; paged variants just take tiles from table-indexed blocks.

questions.q: Near-100% utilization with no preemption under unknown lengths?
questions.a: Open. It's a trade between over-reservation and preemption risk, with no guarantee under heavy-tailed lengths.

questions.q: Provably safe prefix sharing with most of the benefit?
questions.a: Open. k-tenant thresholds, noise, salts and constant-time responses all cost hit rate or latency, and formal guarantees are rare.

questions.q: Will hardware VM replace software block tables?
questions.a: Open. vAttention is competitive, but page granularity and the lack of hardware CoW limit it. Software tables remain the default in vLLM, TRT-LLM and SGLang as of 2026.
